candidates.label: Tell es-Sultan (Old Testament-era mound)
candidates.support: Wikidata's coordinate agrees with the Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire's point to within about 200 meters and with Pleiades' representative point to within about 70 meters. This point represents the pre-exilic and Old Testament-era city; the Gospel-era episodes below are set at the separate Herodian/Roman-period site about 2 km south (see the second candidate).

candidates.label: Tulul Abu al-'Alayiq (Hasmonean/Herodian winter palace complex)
candidates.support: This is the Gospel-era city: a Hasmonean and Herodian winter-palace complex about 2 km south of Tell es-Sultan, matching the site the New Testament episodes below (Zacchaeus, the blind man/men, the road to Jericho) are set in or near. OpenBible.info's own place record for the New Testament-era Jericho resolves to this same site, independently confirming the identification; no separate DARE or Pleiades numeric ID could be found cataloging this complex apart from the main Jericho entries above.

summary.text: Jericho lies in the Jordan Valley north of the Dead Sea, in a desert oasis watered by the perennial spring of 'Ain es-Sultan, and is one of the most anciently inhabited sites in the region. By the first century AD the inhabited city had shifted about two kilometers south of the Old Testament-era mound, Tell es-Sultan, to a new site that the Hasmoneans, a line of Jewish kings, and later the family of Herod the Great built up as a winter palace complex. The Jewish historian Josephus praises the oasis's many kinds of palm trees, its balsam and its cypress trees, writing that whoever called the place divine "would not be mistaken."

history.text: The Gospels set several episodes on the road through or near the city: Jesus healing a blind man, or two men, and his encounter with Zacchaeus, "a chief tax collector" who "was rich." Luke's parable of the Good Samaritan begins with a man "going down from Jerusalem to Jericho." Hebrews recalls that the walls of Jericho "fell down after they had been encircled for seven days," and credits this to faith.

Much later, a palace complex now known as Hisham's Palace was built at Khirbat al-Mafjar, just north of the city, with baths and a water system of aqueducts, bridges and a mill that its surveyors date to the Umayyad, or early Islamic, period.

Today Jericho is a town around the ancient oasis, and the spring of 'Ain es-Sultan still serves as a water source. Visitors can see the excavated Hasmonean and Herodian winter palaces, the mound of Tell es-Sultan, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and national archaeological park just northwest of the modern town, and Hisham's Palace to the north.

scripture.textWEB: As they went out from Jericho, a great multitude followed him.
They came to Jericho. As he went out from Jericho with his disciples and a great multitude, the son of Timaeus, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, was sitting by the road.
Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
As he came near Jericho, a certain blind man sat by the road, begging.
He entered and was passing through Jericho.
There was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector, and he was rich.
By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days.
Behold, two blind men sitting by the road, when they heard that Jesus was passing by, cried out, “Lord, have mercy on us, you son of David!”

otConnections.note: The account of Jericho's walls falling during Joshua's conquest is the Old Testament's best-known episode set at the site and is referenced in the New Testament at Hebrews 11:30.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Ethnarchy of Judea, Samaria and Idumea (ruler: Herod Archelaus)
politicalHistory.note: The emperor Augustus did not grant Archelaus the royal title his father's will asked for, only "ethnarch." The first-century Jewish historian Josephus adds that Augustus took Gaza, Gadara and Hippos from Archelaus's share and added them to the province of Syria. The map doesn't draw Gaza's land separately, so it shows Gaza, and the coast south-west of it as far as Egypt, with this area.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Prefects, e.g. Pontius Pilate)
politicalHistory.note: Luke links a census "when Quirinius was governor of Syria" to Jesus' birth, which Luke and Matthew place in Herod's days; the Jewish historian Josephus dates Quirinius's own census of Judea to this year. This map takes no position on how the accounts relate. The map shows Gaza and the coast south-west of it, as far as Egypt, with this area, since it doesn't draw them separately.
